case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal candidates have Article III standing to challenge Illinois’s practice of counting mail ballots received after the federal Election Day set by Congress when those ballots are timely postmarked or certified as cast by Election Day.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Day statutes: 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 (House and Senate elections held on a single congressionally set day) and 3 U.S.C. §§ 1, 21(1) (Presidential electors chosen on a single day); Illinois provision authorizing counting of certain mail ballots received up to two weeks after Election Day: 10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c) (2025).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (federal candidates and aligned parties) argue they suffer a concrete, particularized injury when Illinois counts ballots received after the federally mandated Election Day, because post–Election Day receipt/processing allegedly dilutes or distorts the legally valid vote total, increases the risk of unlawful ballots being included, and can alter outcomes or campaign strategy in close races. They contend federal law requires the election to be completed on the single federal Election Day (not merely initiated), making Illinois’s two-week receipt window unlawful, and they assert candidates are proper parties to sue because they are direct competitors in the election whose chances of winning are affected by the inclusion of allegedly unlawful votes.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Illinois election officials) argue petitioners lack standing because their claimed injury is speculative, generalized, and not traceable to the challenged receipt-and-counting rule in a way that satisfies Article III. They maintain that counting timely cast mail ballots that arrive after Election Day does not necessarily violate federal law and does not inflict a cognizable candidate-specific injury absent a showing that the rule will likely change the election’s outcome or otherwise cause a concrete competitive harm. They also emphasize that election administration choices like receipt deadlines are traditionally within state authority and that petitioners’ theory resembles an impermissible 'generalized grievance' about compliance with election law.

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain with Respondent because petitioners never get past Article III’s threshold requirements: their asserted competitive injury and “vote dilution” rest on a chain of contingencies about the number of late-arriving ballots, how they break, and whether they will matter in any petitioner’s race, which Clapper and Gill treat as too speculative and too abstract. Justice Barrett is right that even assuming a statutory violation, illegality does not itself supply the missing concrete, particularized injury, nor does it cure redressability where an injunction would not likely change petitioners’ electoral prospects without further non-speculative allegations. The strongest petitioner argument—competitor standing whenever counting rules change—lacks an administrable limiting principle on this record because the challenged receipt window applies symmetrically and is untethered to race-specific harm. Consistent with Steel Co., we should resolve the case on standing and avoid issuing an advisory opinion on the merits of the Election Day statutes.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point is competitor standing—that counting ballots received after Election Day alters the rules of the contest and inflicts a competitive injury. But, as the Chief Justice explains, that theory still rests on contingencies (how many late-arriving ballots there will be, how they break, and whether they matter), which Clapper and Gill treat as insufficiently concrete and particularized. Justice Barrett is correct that an asserted statutory violation does not itself supply injury in fact or redressability; otherwise we would collapse Article III into a free-floating legality review and invite courts to supervise ordinary election administration without objective, manageable limits. Because petitioners have not tied the receipt window to a likely, race-specific harm, we should dismiss for want of standing and avoid reaching the merits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point remains the competitor-standing theory: that counting ballots received after Election Day alters the terms of the contest and inflicts a competitive injury. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, that asserted injury still turns on a speculative chain—how many late-arriving ballots there will be, how they will break, and whether they will be outcome-significant for any named candidate—so it fails concreteness and particularization under Clapper and Gill, and redressability is similarly conjectural. Justice Thomas is also right that accepting standing on this “illegality/vote dilution” abstraction would effectively collapse injury into the claimed statutory violation and invite federal-court supervision of routine election-administration disputes without a manageable limiting principle. On this record, Steel Co. counsels we stop at Article III and dismiss without reaching the Election Day merits.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point is the competitor-standing theory—that counting ballots received after Election Day alters competitive conditions and thus injures candidates. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, that asserted injury still turns on a chain of contingencies about the number of late-arriving ballots, how they break, and whether they affect any petitioner’s race, which Clapper and Gill do not permit us to treat as concrete and particularized. Justice Barrett’s point is dispositive on this posture: alleged illegality cannot itself supply the missing injury-in-fact or redressability; otherwise we would collapse Article III into a generalized compliance dispute. Consistent with Steel Co., we should dismiss for lack of standing without reaching the statutory merits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest claim is competitor standing: that counting ballots received after Election Day changes the rules of the race and predictably injures candidates. But as the Chief Justice explains, that asserted injury still turns on contingencies—how many late-arriving ballots exist, whether they are outcome-significant in any petitioner’s contest, and how they break—making this look like the kind of plaintiff-unspecific, speculative vote-dilution theory Gill and Clapper reject. Justice Barrett’s point is also dispositive: alleged illegality cannot itself supply injury-in-fact or redressability; Article III requires a concrete, particularized harm plausibly alleged for these candidates, not a generalized compliance objection. Limiting ourselves to what is before us, accepting standing on these allegations would invite federal-court oversight of election administration in the abstract, contrary to the separation-of-powers function our standing cases serve.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point remains competitor standing—that changing the receipt-and-counting rules alters the competitive conditions of the race and thus injures candidates. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, that asserted injury still turns on a chain of contingencies (how many ballots arrive after Election Day, how they are cast, and whether they matter in any petitioner’s contest), which Clapper and Gill tell us cannot substitute for a concrete, particularized, and imminent injury. Even assuming a statutory violation, Justice Barrett is right that illegality does not itself supply injury in fact, and redressability fails for the same reason: an injunction here would not likely remedy any candidate-specific harm without the very speculation Article III forbids. Under Steel Co., we must stop at jurisdiction and dismiss without reaching the Election Day merits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point is competitor standing—that changing the receipt-and-counting rule alters competitive conditions for candidates. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, the alleged injury here still turns on a speculative chain: how many ballots arrive after Election Day, how they break, and whether they are outcome-determinative in any petitioner’s race, which Clapper treats as too conjectural and Gill treats as too abstract. Justice Barrett’s redressability point reinforces that even an injunction against counting those ballots would not likely remedy any candidate-specific injury without the same speculation. Treating the asserted statutory illegality itself as injury would collapse Article III into a generalized compliance suit and undermine the separation-of-powers function of standing.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest petitioner-side point is competitor standing: that changing the receipt-and-counting window alters the competitive conditions of the race. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, the alleged harm still turns on a chain of contingencies—how many ballots arrive late, how they break, and whether they matter in any petitioner’s contest—making the asserted injury too speculative under Clapper and too abstract under Gill. And as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, redressability fails for the same reason: an injunction would not likely change petitioners’ electoral prospects without further, non-speculative allegations tied to their races. Alleged illegality cannot itself “transform” these conjectures into an injury in fact, so I would begin—and end—with standing.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest theory—competitor standing based on an allegedly unlawful expansion of the counted ballot pool—still does not supply the concrete, particularized injury Article III demands on this record. As the Chief Justice explains, their asserted vote-dilution/strategic harms rest on a chain of contingencies about how many late-arriving ballots there will be, how they will be cast, and whether they will be outcome-determinative, which Clapper and Gill reject as too speculative and too abstract. Justice Barrett’s point is also decisive for me: we cannot treat the asserted statutory violation itself as the injury, because that would collapse standing into merits and invite generalized supervision of election administration. On this secure and sufficient jurisdictional ground, I would dismiss without reaching the Election Day merits.

John Roberts.reasoning: Starting with Article III, petitioners have not shown an injury in fact that is concrete and particularized rather than a speculative fear that later-arriving, timely-cast mail ballots might “dilute” their vote totals or alter campaign strategy; Clapper requires more than a chain of possibilities, and Gill underscores that abstract vote-dilution theories unmoored from a plaintiff-specific, likely effect are not enough. Traceability is likewise thin because any asserted competitive harm depends on independent, uncertain contingencies (how many ballots arrive late, whether they are outcome-determinative, and how voters behave), rather than a predictable “pocketbook” or similarly concrete harm caused by the receipt deadline itself. And redressability is conjectural absent a plausible showing that enjoining the two-week receipt window would likely change the petitioner’s electoral prospects, making this look like a generalized grievance about state compliance with federal timing statutes rather than a justiciable candidate-specific injury. Without a clear, non-speculative competitive injury akin to the concrete burdens recognized in candidate-standing cases, the case fails at the threshold and we need not reach the merits of whether federal Election Day statutes forbid counting timely-cast ballots received after Election Day.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ asserted injuries—"vote dilution," increased risk of unlawful ballots, and strategic uncertainty—are not the kind of concrete, particularized harms Article III demands; they read as generalized grievances about the State’s compliance with election law unless tied to a specific, imminent competitive injury (e.g., a likely outcome-determinative number of allegedly unlawful ballots). Accepting standing on this abstract theory would invite federal courts to supervise routine election-administration choices without a clear, objective, administrable benchmark for when a candidate’s “chance of winning” has been legally cognizably impaired, the very sort of indeterminate inquiry Gill cautions against. Moreover, the relief sought would require a federal court to restructure Illinois’s ballot-receipt and counting rules—an exercise of equitable power that risks exceeding traditional bounds and, when imposed close to an election, can “fundamentally alter[] the nature of the election.” Absent a concrete showing that these post–Election Day receipts will likely change the result in petitioners’ races (as opposed to a speculative possibility), the case is not fit for federal judicial resolution.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: At the threshold, petitioners’ theory of injury—“vote dilution” or “distortion” from counting ballots received after Election Day—does not identify a concrete, candidate-specific harm that is certainly impending or likely, as opposed to a generalized grievance about the State’s compliance with election rules. Unlike classic competitor-standing cases where the challenged rule directly changes the competitive conditions for the plaintiff (e.g., by regulating fundraising or ballot access), Illinois’s receipt-and-counting window affects all candidates symmetrically and, on this record, petitioners do not plausibly allege that the number of ballots arriving after Election Day is likely to be outcome-determinative or otherwise to inflict a particularized competitive injury traceable to the rule. Accepting standing on these allegations would effectively allow any federal candidate to litigate any asserted defect in a State’s election administration without the individualized showing Article III requires, something our cases have repeatedly rejected. Because petitioners have not shown a concrete and particularized injury fairly traceable to the challenged practice, the case should be dismissed for lack of standing.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Applying the proper Article III framework, the focus must remain on what petitioners plausibly allege in their complaint as a concrete, particularized injury that is fairly traceable to Illinois’ receipt-and-counting rule and likely redressable by the requested relief. Here, petitioners’ theory largely rests on an abstract claim that counting timely cast ballots received after Election Day “dilutes” lawful votes or might alter outcomes, but without non-speculative allegations that the challenged practice will likely cause them a concrete competitive harm in their specific races rather than a generalized interest in correct application of election law. That sort of asserted injury—premised on the government’s alleged failure to follow the law and on contingent future election scenarios—mirrors the generalized-grievance and speculation concerns this Court has repeatedly rejected, and enjoining the rule would not reliably redress petitioners’ alleged harm absent plausible allegations tying the receipt window to a likely, candidate-specific injury. Courts should not relax standing in election cases by presuming injury from purported illegality; jurisdiction turns on pleaded facts, not on broad assumptions about election administration.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III demands a concrete, particularized injury, and petitioners’ theory—“vote dilution” from counting ballots received after Election Day even when timely cast—reads as an undifferentiated grievance that the State is not following federal law, not a personal injury to these candidates. Petitioners do not plead facts showing that Illinois’s two-week receipt window will likely change any particular race they are in, or otherwise impose a non-speculative competitive harm; at this stage, their asserted injury depends on a chain of contingencies about how many late-arriving ballots there will be, how they will break, and whether they will matter. Our experience with election administration also counsels against converting every disputed counting rule into candidate standing absent a concrete showing of likely effect, because that would invite federal courts to supervise election-law compliance in the abstract. Holding only what is before us, these allegations are too conjectural to satisfy imminence and particularization, so the case must be dismissed for lack of standing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III permits us to resolve only an “actual case,” not a dispute over whether Illinois’s election rules conform to petitioners’ preferred reading of federal law. Petitioners’ asserted injuries—vote “dilution,” heightened “risk” of unlawful ballots, and altered campaign strategy—are framed at a high level of generality and, on this record, remain speculative and not particularized to these candidates absent allegations that the challenged two-week receipt window will likely change their election outcomes or inflict a concrete competitive harm. Even assuming some injury, redressability is missing: an order forbidding Illinois from counting timely cast ballots received after Election Day would not necessarily remedy any candidate-specific harm without speculation about how many ballots are affected, for whom they would be cast, and whether they would be outcome-determinative. Because standing fails at least on concreteness and redressability, we cannot proceed to the merits under Steel Co.’s jurisdiction-first rule.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III requires petitioners to show a concrete, particularized injury to them—not an abstract claim that Illinois is administering elections unlawfully. Here, the candidates’ asserted harms (vote “dilution,” increased risk of unlawful ballots, altered campaign strategy) are largely speculative and contingent on uncertain future events—e.g., that enough late-arriving but timely cast ballots will be counted to affect results or otherwise inflict a concrete competitive harm—rather than an injury that is actual or certainly impending. Petitioners also have not supplied evidence tying any concrete injury to Illinois’s receipt-and-counting window as opposed to generalized disagreement with the State’s election rules, and the requested relief would risk converting the federal courts into a forum for advisory opinions about election administration. Under separation-of-powers principles and our standing precedents, that is insufficient to establish injury in fact (and therefore traceability and redressability) for this suit.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: We begin—and end—with standing. Petitioners’ asserted harms (vote dilution, increased risk of unlawful ballots, altered campaign strategy) are pleaded at a high level of generality and depend on a chain of contingencies—how many late-arriving ballots will be counted, whether they are outcome-determinative in petitioners’ races, and whether their inclusion will concretely disadvantage these particular candidates—making the alleged injury too speculative under Article III’s requirement of an actual or imminently threatened, particularized harm. Nor have petitioners plausibly shown redressability, because an injunction against counting timely cast ballots received after Election Day would not necessarily change any candidate’s prospects absent allegations that such ballots will likely affect their specific election outcomes, rather than merely asserting a generalized grievance about Illinois’s compliance with federal Election Day statutes. Whatever the merits of petitioners’ statutory theory, it cannot be used to “transform[]” an asserted legal violation into a cognizable injury in fact.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Starting and ending with the most secure and sufficient basis, petitioners have not shown a concrete, particularized injury traceable to Illinois’s receipt-and-counting rule: their “vote dilution/illegality” theory largely amounts to a generalized grievance that the State is not following federal election timing statutes, plus speculation that late-arriving-but-timely-cast ballots will change outcomes or alter campaign strategy in a way that is imminent and likely. Under settled standing principles, Article III does not permit federal courts to adjudicate abstract disputes about legal compliance untethered to a demonstrated, candidate-specific competitive harm in the particular election at issue. Nor can petitioners bypass this problem by reframing the injury as “increased risk” of unlawful ballots; absent factual allegations making that risk certainly impending or at least substantial, it remains conjectural and insufficient. Because standing fails on this narrow ground, the Court need not reach the broader statutory question whether the federal Election Day provisions foreclose States from counting ballots cast by Election Day but received shortly thereafter.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal candidates (and related plaintiffs) have Article III standing to challenge Illinois’s practice of counting mail-in ballots received after the federally prescribed Election Day when timely postmarked or certified as cast by Election Day.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1 and § 21(1)) as applied to Illinois’s post–Election Day ballot-receipt deadline (10 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/19-8(c) (2025)), and Article III standing requirements under the U.S. Constitution.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that federal law sets a single, uniform day for federal elections and that Illinois’s rule requiring acceptance and counting of certain mail ballots received up to roughly two weeks after Election Day unlawfully extends the election beyond that day. They contend this practice dilutes lawful votes and injures candidates (and aligned political entities) by altering the electorate and the tally after the statutory Election Day, and that such competitive/electoral harms are sufficiently concrete and particularized to confer standing to sue state election officials to stop the counting of late-received ballots in federal elections.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the plaintiffs lack Article III standing because their alleged injury is speculative, generalized, and not traceable to or redressable by the requested relief absent concrete facts showing that late-arriving ballots will change an election outcome or otherwise cause a particularized harm to the specific candidates. They maintain that Illinois’s receipt-and-counting rule is a permissible administrative feature of mail voting (treating ballots as cast by Election Day if postmarked/certified by then), and that federal courts should not adjudicate what amounts to a generalized grievance about election administration without a plaintiff showing individualized, non-hypothetical injury.

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain persuaded that we should resolve this on Article III standing. The strongest petitioner argument—recognized by Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch—is that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury whenever allegedly unlawful ballots are counted, without needing to show the outcome will change. But on this record the asserted harm still turns on a speculative chain of contingencies (how many late ballots, for whom, and whether they matter in any plaintiff’s race), defeating injury in fact and redressability under Lujan/Spokeo and risking an advisory opinion about election administration. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, without race-specific, nonconclusory allegations tying “the one Government action that causes” harm to these particular candidates, the case amounts to an undifferentiated grievance in lawful elections.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest petitioner contention is that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury whenever allegedly unlawful ballots are counted, without needing outcome-determinative proof. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, this record supplies no plaintiff-specific, race-specific facts showing a non-speculative likelihood that late-arriving ballots will materially affect any candidate’s own contest; the asserted harm depends on contingencies and third-party choices that defeat traceability and redressability under Lujan. Recognizing standing on this generalized “altered electorate/vote dilution” theory would invite federal courts to supervise election administration in the abstract, exceeding our limited role and risking advisory opinions. I would therefore dismiss for lack of Article III standing and not reach the merits or fashion any novel equitable relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is the “competitive injury/vote dilution” theory—that counting allegedly unlawful late-arriving ballots necessarily alters the electorate and burdens candidates in a way sufficient for standing. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, that asserted harm here rests on a chain of contingencies driven by third parties (voters’ mailing decisions, postal delays, the number of late ballots, and whether they matter in any plaintiff’s race), which defeats traceability and especially redressability under Lujan. Nor does this fit within Lujan’s footnote 7 procedural-right framework because petitioners are not vindicating a concrete, personal stake made cognizable by a procedural entitlement; they are effectively seeking generalized judicial supervision of statewide election administration. I would therefore dismiss for lack of Article III standing and avoid reaching the merits.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioners’ best argument is that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury whenever a State counts allegedly unlawful late-arriving ballots, because that changes the electorate and forces campaigns to respond. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Article III still requires a plaintiff-by-plaintiff, nonconclusory showing that this particular receipt rule plausibly threatens a concrete disadvantage in an identified contest; here the alleged harm turns on contingencies (volume of late ballots, voter preferences, margins) and independent third-party actions that defeat traceability and redressability under Lujan and TransUnion. At the pleading stage, alleging illegality and an abstract “dilution” theory is not enough without factual allegations tying the challenged practice to a likely, imminent competitive harm to these specific candidates. Because the requested injunction would mainly vindicate a preferred reading of federal election statutes rather than redress a demonstrated candidate-specific injury, I would dismiss for lack of standing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is the “competitive injury” theory—that counting ballots after Election Day necessarily alters the electorate and forces campaigns to respond. But as the Chief Justice explains, pitched at that level it becomes indistinguishable from a generalized interest in lawful election administration, and Article III requires a plaintiff-specific, concrete stake rather than an objection in gross. Justice Barrett is also right that the alleged harm depends on a chain of contingencies and third-party actions (mailing behavior, postal delay, and margin sensitivity), which makes traceability and redressability too speculative on this record. Given those defects, I would decide the case on standing and avoid an advisory opinion on the meaning of the federal Election Day statutes.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is the competitor-standing theory: that a candidate suffers concrete harm when allegedly unlawful ballots are added to the electorate, even absent proof of outcome determinativeness. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, Article III still requires a plaintiff-by-plaintiff showing that this challenged receipt rule is likely to inflict a non-speculative injury in a particular contest, not an undifferentiated interest in lawful election administration. Justice Barrett’s observation about the causal chain—hinging on independent third-party actions (voter mailing choices, postal delays, and how many ballots arrive late and for whom)—underscores why traceability and especially redressability remain conjectural on this record. History and tradition likewise do not support opening federal courts to statewide election-rule challenges untethered to a demonstrated, individualized injury, so I would dismiss for lack of standing.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest petitioner contention is competitor standing: candidates are injured whenever allegedly unlawful ballots are counted, without needing to show outcome determinativeness. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Article III still requires a concrete, plaintiff-specific injury supported by stage-appropriate facts, and here the asserted “vote dilution/altered electorate” remains an undifferentiated grievance about statewide election administration. Justice Gorsuch’s point about the speculative causal chain—dependent on voters’ mailing choices, postal delays, and unknown margins—underscores why traceability and redressability are conjectural for the particular injunction sought. Because standing is not dispensed in gross and must be claim- and remedy-specific, we should dismiss for lack of jurisdiction and not reach the merits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest petitioner argument is competitor standing: that candidates suffer a concrete competitive injury when allegedly unlawful ballots are counted, even absent proof of outcome determinativeness. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Article III still requires a plaintiff-specific, non-speculative injury tied to the challenged receipt rule, not an abstract claim that the electorate has been “altered.” Here, the alleged harm turns on an uncertain chain of third-party actions—voter mailing choices, postal delays, and the number and distribution of late-arriving ballots—so traceability and redressability remain conjectural under Lujan/Clapper. I would therefore begin—and end—with standing and dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is the competitor-injury theory: that counting allegedly unlawful late-arriving ballots inflicts a concrete, candidate-specific disadvantage even absent proof of outcome determinativeness. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, this record offers no race-specific, nonconclusory allegations that the challenged receipt rule is likely to add a meaningful number of votes in any identified contest involving these plaintiffs, and the asserted harm depends on a speculative chain of third-party actions (voter mailing choices, postal delays, and officials’ counting decisions). That contingency also undermines redressability in the way Justice Gorsuch flags: an injunction would enforce petitioners’ preferred legal rule in the abstract without a non-hypothetical showing it will likely remedy a plaintiff-specific competitive injury. The secure and sufficient basis for decision is therefore Article III standing, allowing us to avoid unnecessary merits pronouncements about the federal “Election Day” statutes.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III requires plaintiffs to show a concrete, particularized injury fairly traceable to the challenged government action and likely to be redressed by the requested relief. Here the asserted harm—“vote dilution” or an altered electorate from counting mail ballots received after Election Day—operates, on this record, as an undifferentiated grievance shared by all participants in Illinois federal elections unless a candidate plausibly alleges facts showing a non-speculative, personal competitive injury (for example, a race-specific showing that the challenged receipt rule will likely affect that candidate’s vote total or prospects, not merely that the State is administering elections unlawfully). Petitioners have not identified “the one Government action that causes” them a concrete injury in a way that is distinct from the generalized interest in having the State follow federal election statutes, and their requested injunction would not redress any candidate-specific harm absent a showing that late-received ballots are likely to change the result or otherwise impose a particularized competitive disadvantage. Under our precedents, federal courts do not exercise jurisdiction to police compliance with election law in the abstract, and these allegations fall on the generalized-grievance side of the line.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Before reaching any merits dispute about the meaning of the federal Election Day statutes, I would hold these plaintiffs lack Article III standing because they allege, at most, an undifferentiated grievance that Illinois is not following federal law and a generalized “vote dilution” theory shared by all timely voters. Nothing in the record, as framed here, supplies a concrete, candidate-specific injury—such as facts showing that identifiable late-received ballots will likely alter the result in the particular federal race(s) at issue—so the asserted harm remains speculative and not sufficiently particularized under our cases. Nor is redressability shown: an injunction halting the counting of a category of ballots absent a demonstrated, race-specific causal connection asks the federal courts to supervise election administration in a way that exceeds the limited judicial role, especially where the alleged injury is not uniquely personal to these candidates. Consistent with our insistence on threshold justiciability limits, this case should be dismissed for lack of standing rather than used as a vehicle for broad judicial control of state election practices.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III requires a plaintiff to show a concrete and particularized injury that is actual or imminent, fairly traceable to Illinois’s post–Election Day receipt rule, and likely to be redressed by an injunction. On the facts presented, the asserted “vote dilution” and competitive-harm theories rest on speculation that late-received ballots will be numerous, outcome-affecting, or otherwise impose a candidate-specific injury, which is too generalized and contingent to satisfy Lujan’s injury-in-fact and redressability requirements. Nor is this a procedural-right case in which Congress has created a litigant-specific procedural entitlement protecting a concrete interest that would relax immediacy or redressability; instead, petitioners advance a broad objection to statewide election administration. Because the candidates and aligned entities have not shown a non-hypothetical, particularized injury traceable to the challenged counting practice, I would find no standing and vote to affirm dismissal.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III requires a plaintiff-by-plaintiff showing of a concrete, particularized injury, and these candidates’ allegations largely amount to a claim that Illinois is violating a federal Election Day rule and thereby “diluting” votes in the abstract. At the pleading stage, they must allege nonconclusory facts plausibly connecting the post–Election Day receipt deadline to a cognizable competitive harm to each candidate (e.g., a concrete, imminent risk that identifiable late-arriving ballots will affect their own election), not speculation that counting additional ballots might change results in some race. Absent such factual allegations, the asserted injury resembles a generalized grievance about election administration—precisely the kind of suit Gill cautions federal courts not to entertain as a vehicle for vindicating broad political interests. Because the requested injunction would not redress any plaintiff-specific harm on this record beyond enforcing their preferred reading of the statute, the case should be dismissed for lack of standing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III demands that these federal candidates and aligned entities show a concrete and particularized injury to themselves, not a generalized objection to how Illinois runs an election. On the pleaded facts, the claimed “vote dilution” and “altered electorate” theories depend on speculation that a measurable number of timely-cast but later-received ballots will be counted and will disadvantage these particular candidates in a way distinct from the public at large—precisely the kind of undifferentiated, outcome-contingent grievance our cases reject. Nor does alleging prospective campaign expenditures to respond to post–Election Day counting suffice absent a record-based showing that Illinois’s receipt deadline actually imposes a non-hypothetical, candidate-specific burden rather than the ordinary incident of electoral competition. Because plaintiffs have not demonstrated an injury that is actual or imminent, fairly traceable to the challenged practice, and redressable by an injunction, the suit falls outside the federal courts’ proper role.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III permits us to decide only concrete cases, and these plaintiffs have not carried their burden under Lujan to show an injury to their own legally protected interests that is concrete and particularized rather than an abstract objection to how Illinois administers mail voting. Their asserted “vote dilution/competitive harm” depends on the independent choices of third-party voters and on the contingent possibility that a sufficient number of timely-mailed-but-late-received ballots will affect a relevant contest, leaving traceability and especially redressability too speculative on this record. Even if we ordered Illinois to stop counting such ballots, plaintiffs have not shown that relief would likely change their electoral prospects or otherwise remedy a distinct, individualized harm as opposed to simply aligning state practice with their view of federal law. History and tradition also counsel caution before recognizing standing for this sort of generalized, outcome-untethered challenge to election administration brought without a race- or contest-specific showing of concrete injury.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III standing is a threshold, jurisdictional requirement, and these plaintiffs must show a concrete, particularized, and actual or imminent injury—supported by stage-appropriate evidence—not a generalized objection to allegedly unlawful election administration. On this record, the asserted “vote dilution/competitive harm” from counting timely cast but later-received mail ballots is too speculative and not tied to any specific federal race outcome or to a nonconjectural likelihood that the Illinois receipt deadline will cause these particular candidates to lose, change their vote totals in a concrete way, or otherwise inflict a personal injury. Standing is not dispensed in gross: plaintiffs must demonstrate standing claim-by-claim and remedy-by-remedy, and they have not shown that an injunction barring counting of such ballots would likely redress a concrete injury to them rather than simply resolve an abstract legal dispute about the meaning of Election Day statutes. Allowing suit on this showing would risk converting the federal courts into bodies issuing advisory opinions on election rules, contrary to Article III’s case-or-controversy limitation and separation of powers.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: We begin—and end—with standing. On the record described, the candidates’ asserted injury from Illinois’s counting of ballots received after Election Day (but timely postmarked or certified) is framed at too high a level of generality and depends on a speculative chain: that a meaningful number of such ballots will arrive late, will be counted, and will affect the plaintiffs’ electoral prospects in a concrete, particularized way. That causal chain also turns on independent third-party actions (voter choices and the postal system), weakening traceability to the defendants’ challenged conduct, and the requested injunction would not necessarily redress the alleged “dilution” absent a showing that excluding these ballots would likely change or avert a concrete harm to these specific candidates. Without evidence of an actual or imminent, particularized competitive injury to a plaintiff-candidate in a given election context, the suit amounts to a generalized grievance about election administration that Article III does not permit federal courts to adjudicate.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III demands a concrete, non-hypothetical injury, and these plaintiffs’ asserted “vote dilution/competitive harm” rests on an uncertain chain of events—how many ballots will arrive after Election Day, whether they will be counted, and whether they will meaningfully affect any particular candidate’s prospects—making the alleged harm too speculative to qualify as an imminent injury. Redressability is likewise deficient because an injunction barring the counting of timely-cast but later-received ballots would not reliably remedy any candidate-specific injury absent plausible allegations that such ballots are likely to change outcomes in the elections at issue, rather than merely adjust totals in an indeterminate way. Allowing standing on these generalized objections to election administration would risk turning federal courts into overseers of election rules without “real stakes for real people,” and I would resolve the case on that secure jurisdictional ground rather than reach broader questions about the meaning of the federal Election Day statutes. This approach also applies standing principles evenhandedly, without relying on category-based “commonsense” inferences to relax the injury and redressability requirements for certain election-law plaintiffs.
